idea.body: An equation like sin(x) = 1/2 has more than one answer. Any angle on the unit circle with that exact height works, and the pattern repeats every full turn. For 0 <= x < 2 pi, sin(x) = 1/2 has two solutions, pi/6 and 5 pi/6. Two points on the circle share that height. An inverse trig function like arcsin picks out just one of those, the one in its own restricted range. So arcsin(1/2) is exactly pi/6 and no other angle. A robot's joint solves 2 sin(x) - 1 = 0 for 0 <= x < 2 pi, which means sin(x) = 1/2. So x is pi/6 or 5 pi/6, the two points at height 1/2.

steps: Find the reference angle: cosine equals sqrt(2)/2 at pi/4.
Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III.
In quadrant II, the angle is pi minus the reference angle: pi - pi/4 = 3 pi/4.
In quadrant III, the angle is pi plus the reference angle: pi + pi/4 = 5 pi/4.
The two solutions are x = 3 pi/4 and x = 5 pi/4.

ways.name: The reference angle then all quadrants
ways.when: Use this first for any equation already in the form sin(x) = k or cos(x) = k.
steps: The reference angle is pi/6, since sin(pi/6) = 1/2.
Sine is negative in quadrants III and IV.
Quadrant III gives pi + pi/6 = 7 pi/6. Quadrant IV gives 2 pi - pi/6 = 11 pi/6.
ways.trap: Naming only one quadrant and missing the second solution.

ways.name: The unit circle picture
ways.when: Use this when you would rather see the two solutions than compute them.
steps: Draw the circle and a vertical line at x = -sqrt(3)/2.
That line crosses the circle at two points, one above the x axis and one below.
Those points are at pi - pi/6 = 5 pi/6 and pi + pi/6 = 7 pi/6.
ways.trap: Reading only the point above the axis and missing the mirrored point below it.

figure.alt: A unit circle with a dashed vertical line at x = -sqrt(3)/2, crossing the circle at the two solutions.

frames.caption: Solve cos(x) = -sqrt(3)/2 on the unit circle.
Draw the circle and a vertical line.
That line crosses the circle at two points.
Points are at 5 pi/6 and 7 pi/6.

ways.name: Isolate first, then solve
ways.when: Use this when the trig function is not alone on one side yet.
steps: Solve 2 cos(x) - sqrt(2) = 0 for 0 <= x < 2 pi.
Add sqrt(2) to both sides: 2 cos(x) = sqrt(2).
Divide both sides by 2: cos(x) = sqrt(2)/2.
The reference angle is pi/4, cosine is positive in quadrants I and IV: x = pi/4 or 7 pi/4.
ways.example: Solve 2 cos(x) - sqrt(2) = 0 for 0 <= x < 2 pi.
ways.trap: Solving cos(x) = sqrt(2) instead of dividing by 2 first.
